title: Petraeus Urges India to Build Rapid New Warfare Concept for Two-Front Threat
excerpt: The former CIA director told the NDTV World Summit that India must tailor modern, AI-enabled warfare concepts to its own theatres, with China and Pakistan as the central challenge.
body:
• Former CIA Director David Petraeus told the NDTV World Summit 2026 in New Delhi that India needs a very rapid new concept of warfare, tailored to its own geography and threats.
  • He identified the two-front challenge from China and Pakistan as India's most significant strategic hurdle.
  • Petraeus pointed to lessons from Ukraine and to AI systems acting as tireless staff officers, fusing radar and sensor data for air and missile defence.
  • His session, titled "War in the Time of AI," was part of the summit's third edition, held October 22-23 under the theme "A World Between Orders."

Former CIA Director General David Petraeus has advised India to develop a new concept of warfare very rapidly, arguing that traditional military approaches are increasingly insufficient against adversaries adapting at speed. Speaking at the NDTV World Summit 2026 in New Delhi, the retired four-star general identified the persistent two-front security challenge posed by China and Pakistan as the most significant strategic hurdle facing India, according to Times Now World.

Petraeus, who served in the United States military for over 37 years and later directed the Central Intelligence Agency, is now a partner at KKR and chairman of the KKR Global Institute. His summit session was billed as "War in the Time of AI: How Technology Is Rewriting the Battlefield." The summit's third edition ran October 22-23 under the theme "A World Between Orders," with Prime Minister Narendra Modi delivering the keynote, according to afaqs!.

Tailor the concept to the theatre

The core of Petraeus's advice was that a concept of warfare cannot be imported whole. He argued Indian planners must build a flexible, modern framework that accounts for the specific circumstances of the subcontinent, much as the United States adapts its strategies for different theatres. That means planning across very different environments at once: high-altitude borders, maritime domains and air defence.

Drawing on the war in Ukraine, he said lessons from modern combat — cheap drones, dispersed operations, rapid sensor-to-shooter links — must be adapted, not copied, to maintain deterrence. Awareness gained from watching current conflicts, he argued, should inform India's posture before a crisis forces the lesson.

AI as a staff officer

Petraeus placed artificial intelligence at the centre of the change. He described AI-driven systems and large language models functioning as tireless staff officers, processing vast amounts of data continuously and giving commanders analytical support without human fatigue. In air and ballistic missile defence, he said, autonomous systems could fuse data from radars and acoustic sensors into a single, high-fidelity operational picture, improving situational awareness in data-heavy environments.

The argument aligns with the direction of India's own reforms — theatre commands, network-centric operations and indigenous unmanned systems — but Petraeus's emphasis was on speed of conceptual change, not just procurement. Hardware bought under an old doctrine, his remarks implied, does not produce a new way of fighting.

Why the two-front framing matters

Indian military planners have long treated a collusive China-Pakistan challenge as the hardest case: a crisis on one border drawing forces while pressure builds on the other. Petraeus naming it as India's primary hurdle, at a public summit in New Delhi and alongside sessions with External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar and other senior officials, gives external weight to a framing Indian chiefs have made repeatedly in recent years.

What to watch is whether the advice translates into doctrine and budgets: joint theatre structures, AI-enabled command systems and air-defence integration are the areas where a "new concept" would first become visible. Petraeus offered no timeline beyond urgency — very rapid was the phrase — but his venue ensured the message reached the officials who would have to act on it.
